The Myth of the Million Dollar Challenge | The Daily Grail

For all the hoopla, I think we can positively conclude that the Million Dollar Challenge is a publicity stunt and nothing more. The tests are designed to be unpassable. The challenge only exists so skeptics have something to throw in everyone's face: Take the challenge, they say, and don't worry, the standards will be something mutually agreed upon.

Well, let's rephrase that last part to reflect reality: You say what you can do, the Randi foundation comes back with a test that has several orders of magnitude beyond scientific proof as the standard, and then you can take it or leave it. "Agreed to" is a dodge: The test isn't scientific, it's meant to guarantee failure.

This article is not about the paranormal, per se, but about scientific standards and benchmarks versus what is going on with the James Randi foundation. Specifically, the Million Dollar Challenge benchmarks are so much higher than the standards of scientific proof that if you applied them to conventional science, much of accepted scientific facts would have to be thrown out. Science itself would not pass muster if forced to undergo such a high bar before acceptance.

In other words, it is in no way shape or form a legitimate or scientific test; it's just a publicity stunt used to give skeptics a hammer, and to help them to continue their self-assessed feelings of superiority.

The religion of skepticism - the thing that must never be questioned - is materialism, and like all religions, it needs a hook. The hook for skepticism is the idea that you are better and smarter than everyone else, because you are a skeptic. Skeptics would not appreciate the fact that using similar standards, creationists and others have created unpassable tests for skeptics ...if they even know about those tests. And if they do, they certainly will complain that the challenge is unreasonable and un-winable. Yep... it is! :)

This will not lock you out of using alternative OSes. I'm using Xubuntu right now on a UEFI laptop with Secure Boot enabled. Also, unless they change this, an alternative OS most likely won't even have to go though Microsoft to get access to their signing key like many say. Obviously this is specific to the manufacturer but I think most allow you to import new keys. As far as I know OpenSUSE, for example, uses their own signing key with Secure Boot, but it still uses Secure Boot. Secure Boot simply does not force you to use any specific OS. It just secures the booting process and makes sure you know what is happening if adding a new key or booting an OS signed with an unrecognized key. Unless they change what Secure Boot actually is or all manufacturers just lock you out of adding new keys to boot with, this will not cause any problems for alternative OS users (like myself) as long as the makers of the OS handle things the right way.

Obviously, like I said, they very well could lock you into Windows 10. But if they do things the way described in the article, there shouldn't be any major problems. They're not changing Secure Boot so that new keys can't be added or locking other OSes out from using Microsoft's signing key, they're just making it so you can't use an insecure and outdated method of booting your OS. They should have enforced this with Windows 8 IMO. BIOS booting is from the age of 16-bit Real Mode and before any real malware threats. These days we've got 64-bit Long Mode and complex malware designs which include bootkits. Secure Boot should be enforced, Microsoft is making the right choice here. And I don't exactly love Microsoft. Like I said, I'm a Linux user. I've used Fedora, Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, and even (tried) Gentoo. I've used Windows, but I never stay with it for long. I would be as upset as anyone if I was locked into using it and couldn't use my beloved Linux. But that simply will not happen.

tl;dr - Forcing Secure Boot does not force Windows. For most hardware manufacturers it does not even force OS makers into using Microsoft's signing key.
